The price elasticity of electric power use, as determined from data obtained when electricity prices were declining (until the late 1960's) may not be applicable to situations in which prices are rising. One difficulty has been that most elasticity studies, to date, have been limited to sales of kilowatt-hours and have given no consideration to patterns of peak loads.
Rate structures also may be designed to reduce peak demand without significantly affecting energy use, but there has been no broad base of application of such rate structures from which solid conclusions can be drawn. It is appropriate to note here that pricing arrangements designed to reduce peak-hour demands by shifting some uses of power to off-peak periods may have little effect on total use of electric energy. However, it should also be mentioned that any reduction in capital expenditures for new generating capacity by delaying or retarding peak load growth may be somewhat offset by inflation (assuming that the rate of increase in construction costs exceeds return on alternative investments).
Demand probably is somewhat responsive to price in the long run (i.e., several years), but limited in response during shorter periods. Certain life styles dependent upon electrical usage may take both time and strong incentives to change. Commercial and industrial customers have a sunk investment in electric and non-electric equipment. Operating existing equipment even at higher electric rates may be less expensive than investing in more efficient equipment even though it may involve lower operating costs. It is expensive and difficult to change working hours.
Duke Power is working with municipal water-supply officials in an effort to convince them to do all raw-water pumping during off-peak hours. Water treatment and water processing operations resulting in large demand may also be accomplished during off-peak hours in order to assist Applicant with efforts to reduce the utility's peak demand.
The Applicant will provide commercial and industrial customers having high capacity demands with electronic "kWh" and "time" pulses so that with small investments in auxiliary equipment such customers may obtain an instantaneous reading of demand.
